Resolves #18393

Related: #18304

Each Rail now owns a registered `Neo.dashboard.dock.interaction.RevealStateMachine`. Applications can override its methods and defaults through `Neo.overwrites`, or supply a subclass through `Rail.createRevealMachine()`, while Rail retains input wiring and teardown. The raw constructor path is removed. The existing transition table, timing defaults, hover opt-in and document boundary remain intact.

For a Rail-created machine, `Rail.autoHideRevealOnHover` explicitly supplies the hover flag and takes precedence over the machine default. Configure hover on the Rail/workspace; machine timing defaults apply when Rail supplies no finite override.

Evidence: L2 (real Rail input, Neo registration/overwrite and independently owned timer lifecycle) → L2 required (customization and lifecycle contract). Residual: none for this ticket.

### 🔬 Depth Floor

**Challenge:**

**`revealOnHover` is the one default an application cannot override, and nothing says so.** The two timing configs and the hover flag are handled asymmetrically at construction:

```js
// Rail.mjs:246
dwellMs      : Number.isFinite(me.revealDwellMs) ? me.revealDwellMs : undefined,   // ← may be absent
revealOnHover: me.autoHideRevealOnHover                                            // ← ALWAYS passed
```

`dwellMs` / `graceMs` arrive as `undefined` when Rail has no finite value, and `construct()` deletes them (`RevealStateMachine.mjs:105`), so the class default — **and therefore any `Neo.overwrites` default-override of it** — applies. `revealOnHover` is passed unconditionally from a Rail config defaulting to `false`, and `construct()` coerces it (`:112`). The machine's own `revealOnHover: false` default is consequently never consulted, so an app-wide default-override of it is always defeated. `afterSetAutoHideRevealOnHover` then re-asserts the workspace value on every flip.

**I think the behaviour is correct and should not change.** Hover reveal is an a11y hazard, the class JSDoc says so, and a workspace-level opt-in *should* outrank an application-wide default — that is the safer asymmetry. The finding is that the PR body says applications "can override its methods and defaults through `Neo.overwrites`", and for exactly one default that is not true. A clause in the class JSDoc — *"the workspace opt-in is authoritative; this default is not reachable through `Neo.overwrites`"* — would close the gap between the claim and the surface. Non-blocking, and cheaper to write now than to rediscover from a support question.

Cleared under hunting, listed so the search is auditable: module-level mutable state shared across instances (none); timers surviving teardown (`clearTimer()` is idempotent, called from `destroy()` before `super`); `Rail#destroy` forgetting the machine (it destroys and nulls it at `:508`); a retained raw-constructor alias (`new RevealStateMachine` 1 → 0); and the per-instance leak the singleton case cannot have — covered directly by `DockRail.spec.mjs:93`, *"each Rail owns independent reveal state and cancels only its own pending timer"*, which is the arm I would have asked for.

**Rhetorical-Drift Audit (per guide §7.4):**

- [x] PR description: framing matches the diff, with the one narrow exception raised above as the Depth Floor challenge
- [x] Anchor & Echo summaries: precise; the factory JSDoc states the ownership split — *"Override this factory to supply a specialized owner; Rail retains destruction responsibility"* — which is exactly what the code does
- [x] `[RETROSPECTIVE]` tag: N/A — none claimed by the author
- [x] Linked anchors: `#18304` is cited as the audit that surfaced the candidate, not as authority that this cut was pre-decided

**Findings:** Pass, with the documentation asymmetry noted above.

### 🧠 Graph Ingestion Notes

*   **`[KB_GAP]`**: None. Worth recording the inverse as a pattern: `undefined`-then-deleted config keys preserve an overridable default, while an unconditionally-passed value permanently defeats one. Both appear in the same object literal here, deliberately, and the distinction is invisible unless read against `construct()`.
*   **`[TOOLING_GAP]`**: None observed.
*   **`[RETROSPECTIVE]`**: The correct teardown order is the quiet result. `destroy()` clears the timer *and* nulls `onChange` before `super.destroy()`, so a timer that fires between teardown and collection reaches a null callback instead of a half-deleted instance — `Base#destroy` deletes own properties, so the reverse order would have been a live hazard rather than a style preference. Paired with `Rail#destroy:508` destroying the machine before its own super call, the lifecycle is owned end to end.
